texts.78ca9c6e303d: Objective for processing: This study will examine whether socioeconomic position (SEP) is associated with likelihood of organ donation after death. Individuals who die in hospital deemed suitable for organ donation are described as ‘potential organ donors’ and those who go on to donate their organs constitute ‘actual organ donors’. Currently, individuals from the most deprived quintiles in society make up a greater percentage of those who die in-hospital (Summary Hospital-level Mortality Indicator data) but the socioeconomic position (SEP) of ‘potential organ donors’ as compared to ‘actual organ donors’ is not known. Processing activities: The overall study will analyse combined national Hospital Episodes Statistics (HES) and Office for National Statistics (ONS) mortality data to examine deceased organ donation and SEP in England between 2008 and 2012. It will compare rates of actual organ donation by SEP taking into account the potential organ donor population. Basic descriptors will include the proportion of deceased organ donation, that is, the proportion of potential deceased donors converted to actual donors for each IMD decile, adjusted for age-group, gender and ethnicity. A logistic regression analysis will be performed with the binary outcome variable for each potential organ donor of ‘donation after death’ or ‘no donation after death’, with exposure variable SEP score, adjusting the analysis for possible confounders such as gender, age and ethnicity. This will demonstrate whether SEP is associated with likelihood of organ donation after death In terms of preventing disclosure of any potentially identifiable data, the large sample size and the use and examination of national data makes disclosure a low risk. The estimated sample size is 16,000 and the data will be analysed and presented as a national set, no between centre or geographic variation will be examined or presented. IMD will be analysed and presented in deciles, again reducing the risk of disclosure. The threshold rule will be applied to all groups – if 10 individuals or fewer are in a group then the data will be combined into larger groups. For example, if 5 individuals are in IMD decile 1 for an analysis, the decile data will be combined, analysed and presented as quintiles." This aligns with the HES Analysis Guide and where it differs, is more robust. Basic descriptors will include the proportion of deceased organ donation, that is, the proportion of potential deceased donors converted to actual donors for each IMD decile, adjusted for age-group, gender and ethnicity. A logistic regression analysis will be performed with the binary outcome variable for each potential organ donor of ‘donation after death’ or ‘no donation after death’, with exposure variable SEP score, adjusting the analysis for possible confounders such as gender, age and ethnicity. This will demonstrate whether SEP is associated with likelihood of organ donation after death. Specific outputs expected, including target date: The data will only be used for the purpose described above and not shared with any third party. All outputs will be aggregate analysis with small numbers suppressed. Such outputs may be provided at conferences/ in publications in Europe, therefore permission is sought to include the European Ecomomic Area in the territory of use. No record level data will be shared with any European organisation nor made available on the internet in record level form Analysis outputs: The output variables will be the following: - The socioeconomic position (SEP) (as measured by Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) score) of all 'potential organ donors' (i.e. people who meet the criteria for donating their organs after death). This addresses the question: is SEP associated with the likelihood of an individual being in a situation where they could be an organ donor after death? - The SEP of all 'actual organ donors' (i.e. people who do donate their organs after death). This addresses the question: is SEP associated with the likelihood of an individual donating their organs after death? - The proportion of 'actual organ donors' from 'potential organ donors' at different levels of socioeconomic position ie the conversion of potential donors to actual donors at different levels of socioeconomic deprivation. This address the question: is SEP associated with the likelihood of an individual who is suitable for organ donation after death actually donating their organs? Basic descriptors will include the proportion of deceased organ donation, that is, the proportion of potential deceased donors converted to actual donors for each IMD decile, adjusted for age-group, gender and ethnicity.  A logistic regression analysis will be performed with the binary outcome variable for each potential organ donor of ‘donation after death’ or ‘no donation after death’, with exposure variable SEP score, adjusting the analysis for possible confounders such as gender, age and ethnicity. This will demonstrate whether SEP is associated with likelihood of organ donation after death Study outputs: The aim is to disseminate research outputs widely to make the renal and transplant community aware of our work; highlighting important findings and questions for future research. It is of great importance to us that our findings are brought to the attention of both professionals working in renal medicine, transplantation and health service delivery and service users whose health the research is ultimately aimed at improving, that is, individuals with Chronic Kidney Disease and their families.  We anticipate that preliminary work will be submitted for poster or oral presentation at the annual UK Renal Association, British Transplantation Society and European Renal Association conferences. I aim to publish one paper from this piece of work in a peer-reviewed journal. The findings will also be published by NHS Blood and Transplant, who currently publish an annual report looking at the effect of other variables on organ donation after death (e.g. ethnicity, age) but do not currently look at socioeconomic position.  Findings will be circulated to patient groups in two ways. Firstly, with our patient collaborators we will present findings at Southmead Hospital’s Renal Unit Patient Forum with the aim of inviting patient comment on our findings and inviting service user data interpretation, before planning future intervention studies. In addition, we will submit a summary of our findings to the Bristol Area Kidney Patients Association (BAKPA) regular newsletter. On a national scale, final publications and reports will be highlighted via the NHS Blood and Transplant, British Kidney Patient Association and the UK National Kidney Federation websites. Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date: NHS Blood and Transplant performs an annual Potential Donor Audit which examines the association of a number of variables (including ethnicity and gender) on likelihood of organ donation after death, but it does not examine SEP. This study is designed to fill this gap in knowledge.. If a certain SEP is associated with a lower likelihood of organ donation after death this would be worthy of further investigation to understand the reasons for this. It is anticipated that preliminary work will be submitted for presentation at the annual UK Renal Association, British Transplantation Society and European Renal Association conferences. The aim is to publish one paper from this piece of work in a peer-reviewed journal
